blocks.md: **Manufacturing's share of US nonfarm jobs has fallen steadily since World War II, from about 39% in 1944 to about 9% by 2010. The number of manufacturing jobs, by contrast, stayed roughly flat at 17–19 million from the late 1960s to 2000 and then collapsed to about 11.5 million by 2010 — while real manufacturing value added kept rising.**

blocks.md:
| Period | Manufacturing employment (≈, millions) | Real value added |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1948 | 14 | ≈ $250 billion |
| 1979 (peak) | 19.4 | Rising |
| Late 1990s | 17–17.5 | Rising |
| 2010 | 11.5 | ≈ $1.6–1.8 trillion |
All values read off the lecture charts, approximate.

- **Share vs level**: the falling share since the 1940s reflects structural change toward services — the denominator grew. The *level* only fell sharply after 2000, the period of rapid import growth from China.
- **Output did not fall**: real value added kept rising, so the job decline is about labor per unit of output (productivity, automation, offshoring) as well as competition.
- It is hard to attribute the long decline to China, but plausible that without China's growth the post-2000 contraction would have been slower.
